blocks.text: Since I think it is clear from what has been said that the חולד choled of Moses was the mole, just like the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ chulda and the Arabic خلد [khuld] chuld or chold, it must nevertheless not be concealed that among the Talmudic doctors חולדה chulda is for the most part the weasel. The following passages make this plain. In the tractate Cholin, cited above: חלדה הר בחלדה הדרה בעיקרי בתים דמכסי הכא, "The plunging of the knife in slaughtering is called Chalada, a phrase borrowed from the chulda, which lives in the foundations of houses so as to lie hidden there." This does not fit the mole, which lives only in the fields, but rather the domestic weasel, κατοικίδιον [katoikidion]. To it is everywhere opposed חולדת סנאים or חולדת הסניים, the weasel of the brambles, that is, the wild one: as in Kilaim ch. 8, fol. 32 a b, הקופד וחולדת הסניים, "the hedgehog and the weasel of the brambles." There the Gloss of Maimonides says: וחולדת הסניים חיה דומה לחולדה ממיני השועלים, that is, "The weasel of the brambles is a wild animal similar to the common weasel, among the species of foxes." And in Bava kama ch. 4, fol. 80. 1: מגדלין כלבין כופרין וחתולין וקופין וחולדות סנאים מפני שעושין לנקראת הבית, "It is permitted to keep farm dogs, and cats, and apes, and weasels of the brambles" (which are called חולדות), "because they are made for boring through houses." And a little later: אמר ר׳ יהודה שרצא חרצא ואיכא דאמר חרוא דקטני שקי דרעיא ביני וורדיני, "R. Judah said: It is a cutting reptile (CHARTSA). And there are those who say a boring one (CHARZA), because it has slender legs and feeds among the thickets." Thus in Pliny, [II, 444] book 29, chapter 4: "There are two kinds of weasels: one is wild. They differ in size. The Greeks call them ictides, etc. But this one, which roams about our houses, etc." The very point we have made, that חולדה chulda among the Talmudists is generally the weasel and not the mole, follows from the fact that they hold that this animal strangles children, which no one would say of the mole. To this end a passage is adduced from the tractate Thaanith ch. 1, fol. 8. 1: בא וראה כמה גדולים בעלי אמנה מניין מחולדה ובור ומה המאמין בחולדה ובור כך המאמין בהקב״ה על אחת כמה וכמה, "Come and see how the chulda and the well are reckoned among the great witnesses of faith. And who trusts the chulda [col. 1028] and the well, and would not much more trust God, the Holy One, Blessed be He?" On this passage the Talmudic Glossator relates this little tale: מחולדה ובור שהמיתו שני בני אדם מצוי הוא באגדה מעשה בבחור אחד שנתן אמונתו לריבה אחת שישאנה אמרה מי העיד והיה שם בור א׳ וחולדה אמר הבחור בור וחולדה עדים בדבר לימים עבר על אמונתו ונשא אחרת והוליד שני בנים אחד נפל לבור ומת ואחד נשכתו חולדה ומת אמרה לו אשתו מה מעשה הוא זה שבנינו מתים במיתה משונה ואמר לה כך וכך היה מעשה, "The chulda and the well, by which two people were put to death. The story is found in the Aggada about a certain young man who pledged his faith to a girl that he would marry her. 'Who will be witness?' she said. Now there were a well and a chulda (weasel) there. And the young man said, 'The well and the chulda will be witnesses of the matter.' But some days later the same man broke his faith and married another woman, and when she had borne him two sons, one of them fell into the well and died; the other also died, bitten by the chulda, or weasel. Then, asked by his wife why both sons had died a violent death, he told her how the matter stood." Baal Aruch reports many more circumstances of the same story, among them that the child was a boy, and was strangled by the chulda when already three months old. His words are: וילדה בן זכר כשהגיע לג׳ חרשים חנקתו חולדה, "And she bore a male son, whom the chulda strangled when he had already reached his third month." Likewise, concerning the الزبزب [al-zabzab] zebzeb, a species of larger weasel or ferret, caught at Baghdad in the year of the Hijra 304, the Arabs related above^{e)} انه ياكل اطفالهم [annahu yaʾkulu aṭfālahum] that "it devoured their infants," and bit men's hands and women's breasts. To these must be added what the Talmudists adduce in the comparison of the words חולדה chulda, or חולד choled, and חלד cheled; the latter signifies the world in Ps. XLIX, 2., where men are called יושבי חלד, "inhabitants of cheled, that is, of the terrestrial world." And the doctors dispute among themselves why the earth is called חלד cheled, and ask what it has in common with חולד choled, the animal. And in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Cholin ch. 9, fol. 127 a, someone answers: כל שיש ביבשה יש בים חוץ מן החולדה, "Whatever animal is on land is also in the sea, the chulda alone excepted." Lest this be thought [II, 445] said without grounds, here is a pretty story which the most learned Buxtorf brings forward from the writings of the Rabbis in his Lexicon Talmudicum under the word חלד: "There was an assembly of the princes of the world about proper government. The prince of the sea complained that he did not have enough subjects. He was therefore permitted to seek more from the land, provided he made provision for their food. He cast all land animals into the sea, with the command that they should propagate their kind there too. It was done: hence it is said that all land animals are also in the sea, except that some were changed into a monstrous form. When he came to the weasel, she, standing on the shore, said to the prince of the sea: 'Why will you throw me into the sea again? Do you not see that I am already in the sea?' She said this showing her reflection in the sea. The prince, satisfied, let the weasel go. Hence the Talmudists say that all land creatures are in the sea except the weasel, which escaped by its cunning. And the earth is called חלד cheled because it remained the property of the weasel, which is called חולדה chulda or חולד choled." In the Jerusalem Talmud, at the beginning of the chapter On the eight reptiles, the same question is treated, and some answer exactly what we have just said, that the earth and earthly men are compared with the chulda: לפי שכל מה שיש ביבשה יש בים והרבה מינין יש [col. 1029] בים מה שאין כן ביבשה ואין חולדה בים, "because, although everything that is on land is also in the sea, and there are many species in the sea which are not on land, yet the chulda is not in the sea." The other answer is this: חולדה זו גוררת ומנחת ואינה וודעת למי מנחת כך כל באי העולם גוררין ומניחין ואינן יודעין למי מניחין כמו שנאמר יצבור ולא ידע מי אספם, "The chulda drags many things together and leaves them behind, not knowing for whom she leaves them. So too all the people of the world drag many things together and leave them behind, not knowing for whom they will leave them. As it is said, Psal. CXXXIX, 2., „He will heap up, and will not know who will gather them“." So the Aruch cites these things, which, however utterly trifling, nevertheless serve our purpose. For they show that by the word chulda most Talmudists do not mean the mole. For the mole, which is blind, would not be said to have seen its image in the sea and shown it to others. Nor do we read that it stores and hides anything in its burrows. But this is the nature of the weasel, of which Abdollatiph of Baghdad writes in the place cited above: في طبعه انه يسرق ما وجد من فضة او ذهب كما يفعل الغار [fī ṭabʿihi annahu yasriqu mā wajada min fiḍḍa aw dhahab kamā yafʿalu al-ghār] "It is of its nature to steal whatever silver (or gold) it finds, as mice do." Accordingly this story is told there of the weasel: رجل صاد فرخا منها وحبسه في قفص بحيث تراه امه فلما اراته ذهبت ثم جات وفي فمها دينار فالقته بين يديه كانها تفدي ولدها فلم يتركه لها فذهبت وعادت بدينار اخر حتي بلغت من العدد خمسا فلما [II, 446] ان لا يطلق لها ذهبت وعادت بخرقة كانها تشير الي فراغ حاصلها فلم يكترث بها فلما رات ذلك عادت الي دينار فاخذته منه فخشي الرجل من ذلك فاطلق لها ولدها [rajul ṣāda farkhan minhā wa-ḥabasahu fī qafaṣ bi-ḥaythu tarāhu ummuhu fa-lammā arathu dhahabat thumma jāt wa-fī famihā dīnār fa-alqathu bayna yadayhi kaʾannahā tafdī waladahā fa-lam yatrukhu lahā fa-dhahabat wa-ʿādat bi-dīnār ākhar ḥattī balaghat min al-ʿadad khamsan fa-lammā an lā yuṭlaq lahā dhahabat wa-ʿādat bi-khirqa kaʾannahā tushīr ilī farāgh ḥāṣilihā fa-lam yaktarith bihā fa-lammā raʾat dhālika ʿādat ilā dīnār fa-akhadhathu minhu fa-khashiya al-rajul min dhālika fa-aṭlaqa lahā waladahā] "A certain man caught a young weasel and shut it in a cage, so that the mother could see it. When she had seen it, she went away and came back with a denarius in her mouth, which she threw down before him, as if to ransom her young. But when he did not release it, she went off again and brought other denarii, until she had reached the number five. And when she saw that her young was still not released, she also brought a rag (in which the coins had been), to show that she had exhausted her entire hoard. And when she noticed that she was paid no heed, she went back to the coins to take them back. But the man, struck with fear, returned her young to her." It is clear, therefore, that by the word חולדה chulda the Talmudists for the most part mean the weasel. But their authority in this matter moves us little, since they are not consistent with themselves, and among the Arabs and Syrians chuld [col. 1030] or chulda is the mole; and both the origin of the word and the circumstances of the Mosaic text plainly show that the word must be taken in this sense.
